title: Roger — Opening pacing preview

speaker_instructions.Narrator: Warm, grounded storytelling with clear articulation and natural variation. Let meaningful moments breathe. Avoid a sales pitch or exaggerated drama.
speaker_instructions.Roger: A humble, courageous protagonist. Warm, human, expressive conversation with varied pitch and rhythm. Let vulnerability, curiosity, joy, and growing conviction emerge as appropriate to the line. Never a booming announcer or a monotone. In prayers, speak to God personally. Remembrance is woven into ordinary life, not delivered as a sermon. Let fear and trust coexist.
speaker_instructions.Mother: A mature older mother speaking to her adult son. Warm, gently weathered, affectionate, practical and reassuring. Understated, not theatrical.
speaker_instructions.Rita: Gentle and sincere, with quiet conviction and self-respect. Natural, warm conversation.
speaker_instructions.Tim: An ordinary working man. Friendly and direct, with natural warmth. Let frustration or relief follow the meaning of the line.
speaker_instructions.Rick: A successful middle-aged man, kindly and confident. Speak to the craftsman with respect and natural curiosity.
speaker_instructions.Katie: An assured adult woman, elegant, friendly and candid. Natural conversation, never an advertisement.
speaker_instructions.Katie’s father: An experienced older businessman giving patient, practical advice. Conversational, not an announcer.
speaker_instructions.Factory manager: A gruff factory manager, skeptical and dismissive but believable. No shouting or exaggerated villain voice.
speaker_instructions.Coworker: A skeptical coworker teasing another man with dry disbelief. Natural, not cartoonish.
speaker_instructions.Churchgoer: An older, successful man speaking warmly and thoughtfully to someone he respects. Conversational encouragement, never a sermon or grand prophecy.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger worked until the factory windows reflected the lamps inside.

All day, his needle passed through leather.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
At night, he took small repairs home and stitched beside the kitchen table.

Sometimes he fell asleep with the thread still looped around his finger.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He was careful.

He was dependable.

He worked harder when there was less money, and somehow there was always less money.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
One evening, his mother divided a pot of stew among four bowls.

His youngest brother needed a new sole on his school shoe.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
His sister had an examination fee to pay.

Beneath the salt jar lay a notice from the landlord.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger put his wages on the table and watched his mother count them.

She moved a coin from one pile to another, then moved it back.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He wanted to tell her that one day she would stop doing this.

But he could not see how to make next month different from this one.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Eat before it gets cold.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He lifted his spoon.

He could scarcely swallow.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He did not despise his work.

His mother had taught him that honest work was something to respect.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: But he had begun to confuse the life he knew with the only life he could have.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He called it his fate because he could not bear to keep wanting what seemed impossible.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The following evening, Roger stopped at a church on his way home.

He stood outside for a moment with his repair bag against his leg.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he went in.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He sat near the back.

For several minutes he could only look at his hands.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
There was dark wax in the creases of his fingers, and a fine white scar across one knuckle.

He had asked so much of those hands.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: At last, he bowed his head.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, I’m willing to work. You know I am. But I don’t know what to do differently.
turns.instruction: An exhausted man speaking personally to God. Honest helplessness, clearly voiced, no theatrical sobbing.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
His voice caught.

He waited, then continued.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I want my mother to rest. I want my brother and sister to have a chance. I don’t know how to give them that. Please show me a way. Help me recognize it when it comes.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He had prayed for another shift many times.

This time he was asking to see something he had not seen before.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He stayed until the church began to grow quiet.

Nothing had changed in his pocket when he rose.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Yet he had finally spoken the longing he usually swallowed.

He picked up his bag and walked outside.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Near the steps, a man in a well-cut coat was examining the loose buckle on his shoe.

A car waited by the curb.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: The driver had come around to help, but the man waved him back gently.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger recognized the problem.

The small leather loop holding the buckle had begun to split.

He hesitated, then touched the tools inside his bag.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I could secure that for your journey, if you like. It will need a proper repair afterward.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: The man looked up, then smiled and sat on the low wall beside the steps.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Roger knelt and worked a few careful stitches through the sound part of the leather.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Before drawing the thread tight, he silently asked God for care in his hands.

A few minutes later, the buckle held.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: You noticed that quickly. Do you have a shop?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: No. I stitch in the factory. And do repairs when I can.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The man tested the fastening and asked what he owed Roger for the work.

Roger named a modest price.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: The man paid it, then remained beside him while Roger put away his tools.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: Have you thought about taking customers of your own?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: People like me don’t usually get that far.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The man did not laugh.

That made it easier for Roger to say the rest.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: My family depends on me. I can’t afford to dream and leave them hungry.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: Then keep caring for them. But be careful about what you call impossible.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He looked down at the fastening Roger had repaired.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: A few minutes ago, you saw a way to help me that I couldn’t see. How many other things might be possible that you haven’t learned to see yet?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I wouldn’t know where to begin.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: That is different from there being nowhere to begin. You know the limits of what you’ve tried, Roger. You don’t know the limits of what’s possible. And God has no limits.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger glanced back toward the church door.

The words touched the very place from which his prayer had come.

turns.speaker: Churchgoer
turns.text: What would you dare to build if you stopped assuming the answer was already no?

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
The driver opened the car door.

The man thanked Roger again and left.

He had offered no investment, no position, no promise that everything would work.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger remained beside the steps with the payment in his palm.

His circumstances were almost exactly as they had been when he entered the church.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: But a question had entered them.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: That night, after finishing his brother’s shoe, Roger let himself picture a different evening at home.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
His mother putting away the household accounts without a crease between her eyes.

His sister paying her examination fee on time.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: A table with enough for everyone, and something left to offer a guest.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Then he pictured a workshop.

Light over a clean bench.

Good leather.

Customers who came because something he made had improved their lives.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Enough money to pay skilled people well, and enough freedom to choose what he would make next.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
For a moment, the wanting frightened him.

Who was he to imagine such a life?

He almost pushed the picture away.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he remembered the man’s question.

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: God, this is what I want. I want to provide generously. I want to make something useful and live fully. Help me bring these desires to You without shame. Guide what I do with them.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He could see the end of his wages.

He could not see the end of God’s abundance.

God’s knowledge did not stop where Roger’s knowledge stopped.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He had been bringing a small picture of the world into every prayer: a few fortunate people, a fixed number of chances, everyone else waiting for what remained.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Yet the One he prayed to was infinite.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
Roger took a scrap of paper.

At the top, he wrote that he wanted a workshop which supported his family by doing work people truly valued.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Then he began working backward.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
A workshop would need customers.

Customers would need a reason to trust him.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: Before any of that, there would have to be one person whose problem he could help solve.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
He could look for that person before he owned a shop.

He could begin while keeping his factory shifts.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He wrote one thing he could do tomorrow: speak to someone outside the factory, ask what troubled them about their shoes, and listen.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
His mother found him looking at the paper.

He showed her what he had written.

turns.speaker: Mother
turns.text: Can you begin without leaving us hungry?

turns.speaker: Roger
turns.text: I think I can begin small.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: She sat beside him while he worked out what he could spare.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: He put aside a little money, arranged to buy discarded leather with permission, and chose an evening for his first outing.
